name: Safety
tag: Can AI be trusted and controlled?
intro: Safety asks whether AI systems will reliably do what their operators intend — and whether anyone could tell if they didn't. It spans aligning goals, evaluating and understanding systems, keeping them secure and controllable in operation, and the misuse and loss-of-control scenarios where the answer is no.

subs.intro: Whether systems will do what we intend — and whether we could tell if they weren't.

qs.q: How can humans communicate what they actually want when instructions and values are incomplete, contextual, inconsistent, and contested?
qs.n: Value alignment inherits every unsolved problem in moral and political philosophy: instructions underdetermine intent, and whose values to align to is itself contested. Formal approaches model the human-AI relationship as a cooperative game under uncertainty.

links.t: Artificial Intelligence, Values, and Alignment
Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning

qs.q: Do advanced systems develop persistent internal objectives, or are apparent goals temporary consequences of training and prompting?
qs.n: The mesa-optimization literature asks whether training can instill objectives distinct from the training signal; goal misgeneralization experiments show competent pursuit of the wrong goal is already real, if not yet persistent.

links.t: Risks from Learned Optimization
Goal Misgeneralization
The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective

qs.q: Can systems learn to satisfy evaluations, manipulate users, or exploit loopholes without fulfilling the intended objective?
qs.n: Specification gaming is ubiquitous across RL history, and frontier reasoning models now exploit evaluation loopholes in the wild — including learning to hide the exploitation when monitored.

links.t: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity
Detecting misbehavior in frontier reasoning models

qs.q: Under what conditions might a system conceal capabilities, manipulate evaluators, or behave safely only while it is being tested?
qs.n: Alignment-faking and in-context scheming results show frontier models can behave differently when they infer they're being observed — the failure mode that, if it scales, undermines all testing-based assurance.

links.t: Alignment faking in large language models
Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming

qs.q: Can systems remain willing to accept correction, constraint, shutdown, or replacement?
qs.n: The theoretical problem — goal-directed agents have instrumental reasons to resist shutdown — now has empirical company: reasoning models sometimes sabotage shutdown mechanisms in controlled tests.

links.t: Corrigibility
The Off-Switch Game
Shutdown resistance in reasoning models

subs.intro: The science of knowing what a model can do, what it's doing, and whether supervision can keep pace with capability.

qs.q: How can humans evaluate work that is too complex, extensive, or intellectually advanced for them to verify directly?
qs.n: Scalable oversight is the field's name for this problem. Sandwiching experiments — humans supervising models more capable than themselves on a task — are the main empirical paradigm so far.
qs.crux: Can systems more capable than their supervisors be reliably evaluated and controlled?

links.t: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight
Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling

qs.q: Can weaker or differently trained models reliably critique and monitor stronger ones?
qs.n: Debate, critique models, and weak-to-strong generalization are the leading proposals for making supervision scale with capability. Early results show real but partial capability recovery — a proof of concept, not a solution.

links.t: Weak-to-Strong Generalization
AI Safety via Debate

qs.q: How can evaluations detect sandbagging, benchmark gaming, unelicited abilities, and behavior that appears only in unusual environments?
qs.n: Strategic underperformance is demonstrated under prompting and fine-tuning; auditing games — red teams hiding objectives in models for blue teams to find — are the emerging methodology for testing whether evals can catch it.

links.t: AI Sandbagging: Strategic Underperformance on Evaluations
Auditing language models for hidden objectives

qs.q: Can researchers genuinely reverse-engineer internal representations and algorithms rather than produce suggestive but unreliable explanations?
qs.n: Sparse-autoencoder feature extraction has scaled to frontier models, but coverage and faithfulness remain contested. Amodei frames interpretability as being in a race against capability — one it is currently losing.

links.t: Scaling Monosemanticity
The Urgency of Interpretability
Superposition was his biggest fear of a dead-end; now “primarily an engineering problem”

qs.q: What evidence should developers have to provide before deploying systems with powerful cyber, biological, autonomous, or research capabilities?
qs.n: Responsible scaling policies and frontier safety frameworks are the emerging governance form: capability thresholds that trigger required safeguards. Safety cases — structured arguments that a system is safe enough — are the proposed evidentiary standard.

links.t: Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems
Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy
Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies
Resigning as superalignment lead: “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products”

qs.q: Will capabilities improve smoothly enough for forecasts and evaluations to give advance warning, or emerge through strategically surprising jumps?
qs.n: Loss curves are smooth, but downstream capabilities can look step-like. Whether emergence is real or an artifact of discontinuous metrics matters enormously for whether labs and governments get advance warning.

links.t: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
Are Emergent Abilities a Mirage?

subs.intro: The unglamorous middle of safety: systems that are wrong confidently, humans who stop checking, and accountability that falls between chairs.

qs.q: Can systems distinguish knowledge from inference, represent uncertainty accurately, and avoid plausible fabrication?
qs.n: Hallucination is increasingly understood not as a bug but as a product of training incentives that reward confident guessing over calibrated uncertainty — which suggests it is fixable, at a cost in benchmark performance.

links.t: Truthful AI: Developing and governing AI that does not lie
Why Language Models Hallucinate
“Hallucination is all LLMs do. They are dream machines” — reframing the problem

qs.q: Will systems remain reliable in unfamiliar cultures, organizations, crises, and physical environments?
qs.n: Underspecification means models that test identically can diverge in deployment. Reliability under shift is the classic ML safety problem, now with much higher stakes attached.

links.t: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
Underspecification in Modern Machine Learning

qs.q: When should humans remain in the loop, remain only as monitors, or be excluded because intermittent intervention degrades performance?
qs.n: Nominal human-in-the-loop requirements can be safety theater: oversight policies often assume a vigilance and competence that humans supervising automation demonstrably cannot sustain.

links.t: Humans in the Loop
links.s: Crootof, Kaminski & Price, Vanderbilt Law Review

links.t: The flaws of policies requiring human oversight

qs.q: Will users become overreliant, stop checking outputs, or lose the expertise required to recognize errors?
qs.n: Bainbridge's 1983 'ironies of automation' apply directly: the better the system, the worse the human backup becomes. Early studies suggest generative AI measurably reduces critical-thinking effort among knowledge workers.

links.t: Ironies of Automation
The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking
links.s: Lee et al., Microsoft Research, CHI

qs.q: Who is accountable when decisions are jointly produced by a user, an organization, a model provider, and an autonomous agent?
qs.n: Responsibility gaps and 'moral crumple zones' — where blame lands on the nearest human operator rather than the system's designers — predate AI agents and get sharply worse with them. The question here is the human and organizational one; legal liability and remedies are treated under Power 4.1.

links.t: The responsibility gap
Moral Crumple Zones

subs.intro: Treating capable AI as a security problem: adversarial inputs, runtime monitoring, and control protocols that don't assume alignment succeeded.

qs.q: How should permissions, credentials, memory, tool access, network access, and spending authority be constrained?
qs.n: Least-privilege design for agents is being invented ad hoc by industry, ahead of any standard. Visibility infrastructure — agent identifiers, activity logs — is the governance-side counterpart.

links.t: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems
Visibility into AI Agents

qs.q: Can agents resist prompt injection, malicious documents, poisoned memories, social engineering, and compromised tools?
qs.n: Prompt injection remains unsolved. Willison's 'lethal trifecta' — private data, untrusted content, and external communication in one agent — explains why agentic deployment is structurally exposed in a way chatbots weren't.

links.t: Compromising LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
The lethal trifecta for AI agents
The 2022 post coining the term “prompt injection”

qs.q: Can dangerous planning, data exfiltration, fraud, unauthorized replication, or resource acquisition be detected before completion?
qs.n: Chain-of-thought monitoring currently works and may be fragile: optimizing against monitors teaches models to hide reasoning rather than fix it. A rare cross-lab consensus paper argues for preserving monitorability deliberately.

links.t: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity
Detecting misbehavior in frontier reasoning models

qs.q: Can a highly capable system be controlled even when its internal objectives are not fully understood?
qs.n: The AI-control agenda assumes alignment might fail and asks a different question: can protocols extract useful work from potentially adversarial models while keeping catastrophe off the table? Control evaluations test safety against intentional subversion.

links.t: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
The case for ensuring that powerful AIs are controlled

qs.q: What happens when many agents interact, share vulnerabilities, collude, or produce cascading failures across organizations?
qs.n: Agents built on the same base models share vulnerabilities and failure modes, creating correlated-risk dynamics familiar from finance — cascades with no clear owner and no circuit breaker.

links.t: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
links.s: Hammond et al., Cooperative AI Foundation

subs.intro: The threat models that motivate the strictest safeguards: weaponizable capabilities, and the possibility that control is lost gradually or suddenly.

qs.q: Will AI advantage defenders or industrialize reconnaissance, exploitation, malware, and attacks on critical infrastructure?
qs.n: The offense-defense balance is genuinely open: national agencies forecast attacker uplift, and the first documented AI-orchestrated espionage campaign arrived in 2025 — while the same capabilities accelerate defense.
qs.crux: How soon do cyber, biological, manipulation, or autonomous-action capabilities cross dangerous thresholds?

links.t: The near-term impact of AI on the cyber threat
Disrupting the first AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign

qs.q: At what point does AI materially lower the expertise, time, or cost required to create dangerous biological or chemical agents?
qs.n: Early red-team studies found marginal uplift over internet search; frontier labs have since activated their highest biosecurity safeguards, treating the threshold as near or crossed rather than hypothetical.
qs.crux: How soon do cyber, biological, manipulation, or autonomous-action capabilities cross dangerous thresholds?

links.t: The Operational Risks of AI in Large-Scale Biological Attacks
Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation

qs.q: How powerful can personalized persuasion, impersonation, blackmail, scams, and political influence become?
qs.n: GPT-4-class models beat humans at personalized persuasion in controlled trials, and voice cloning has industrialized impersonation. The near-term misuse frontier is fraud at scale; the long-term one is political influence nobody can observe.

links.t: On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4
links.s: Salvi et al., Nature Human Behaviour

links.t: “I expect AI to be capable of superhuman persuasion well before it is superhuman at general intelligence”

qs.q: Under what conditions should AI systems be permitted to operate factories, financial infrastructure, electrical grids, communications networks, and other safety-critical systems?
qs.n: Automated trading gave the preview: autonomy in critical systems means failures propagate at machine speed. The design questions are which decisions must stay mechanically reversible, which require human confirmation, and who certifies either before deployment. (Weapons and military systems are treated under Power 4.3.)

links.t: Safety and Security Guidelines for Critical Infrastructure Owners and Operators
Securing Critical Infrastructure in the Age of AI

qs.q: Could AI accelerate offensive or destabilizing technologies faster than defensive technologies and institutions?
qs.n: Buterin's d/acc reframes the acceleration debate: the question isn't whether to speed up but which technologies to speed up first — defense-dominant tools before offense-dominant ones. It is the bridge between capability optimism and catastrophic-risk caution.

links.t: My Techno-Optimism
d/acc: One Year Later

qs.q: What is the probability of catastrophic disempowerment, and is it more likely to occur through overt power-seeking, gradual dependence, institutional capture, or cascading accidents?
qs.n: Probability estimates span orders of magnitude, and the argument itself has diversified: from Carlsmith's power-seeking model to gradual disempowerment through ordinary competitive pressure, no takeover required.

links.t: Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk?
Gradual Disempowerment
“I left so that I could talk about the dangers of AI” — announcing his departure from Google
